sections.normalized_html: The [MATH: 12]th root of unity [MATH: e^{2\pi \text{i}/3}] can be written as [MATH: e^{2\pi \text{i}/3} = z^p,] where [MATH: z] is the principal [MATH: 12]th root of unity. What is the value of [MATH: p?]

The [MATH: 12]th root of unity [MATH: e^{2\pi \text{i}/3}] can be written as
[MATH: e^{2\pi \text{i}/3} = z^p,]
where [MATH: z] is the principal [MATH: 12]th root of unity. What is the value of [MATH: p?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the [MATH: 12]th roots of unity can be written in the form

[MATH: e^{2 k\pi \text{i} / 12}]

where [MATH: k=0,1,\ldots,11.]

We obtain the principal [MATH: 12]th root of unity by substituting [MATH: k=1{:}]

[MATH: z= e^{2 \cdot 1 \cdot \pi \text{i} / 12} = {\color{blue}e^{\pi \text{i} / 6}}]

We can write the given root of unity as a power of the principal root as follows:

[MATH: e^{2π\textrm{i}/3}|= e^{(2 ⋅ 2π)\textrm{i}/(2 ⋅ 3)}; = e^{4π\textrm{i}/6}; = e^{4 ⋅ π\textrm{i}/6}; = (e^{π\textrm{i}/6})^{4}]

Therefore, [MATH: p={\color{red}4}.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: z] be a [MATH: 7]th root of unity. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: z^7 = 1]

  2. [MATH: (z+z)^7 = 1]

  3. [MATH: z+z=2z] is a [MATH: 7]th root of unity
sections.readable_text:
Let [MATH: z] be a [MATH: 7]th root of unity. Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: z^7 = 1]
2. [MATH: (z+z)^7 = 1]
3. [MATH: z+z=2z] is a [MATH: 7]th root of unity

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. If [MATH: z] is a [MATH: 7]th root of unity, then (by definition), we have that [MATH: z^7=1.]

  • Statement II is false. We have [MATH: (z + z)^{7}|= (2z)^{7}; = 2^{7} ⋅ z^{7}; = 128 ⋅ 1; = 128; ≠ 1.]

  • Statement III is false. From statement II, we have that [MATH: (z+z)^7 \neq 1,] which means that [MATH: z+z=2z] is not a [MATH: 7]th root of unity.

    In general, the sum of two [MATH: n]th roots of unity is not an [MATH: n]th root of unity.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Also, recall that the root corresponding to [MATH: k=1] is the principal [MATH: n]th root of unity.

Content:
We have the following theorem:

Content:
> Any [MATH: n]th root of unity is an integer power of the principal [MATH: n]th root.

Content:

Item 2 — Example: Expressing a Root of Unity Using Its Principal Root

Example Prompt:
The [MATH: 12]th root of unity [MATH: e^{2\pi \text{i}/3}] can be written as
[MATH: e^{2\pi \text{i}/3} = z^p,]
where [MATH: z] is the principal [MATH: 12]th root of unity. What is the value of [MATH: p?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the [MATH: 12]th roots of unity can be written in the form

[MATH: e^{2 k\pi \text{i} / 12}]

where [MATH: k=0,1,\ldots,11.]

We obtain the principal [MATH: 12]th root of unity by substituting [MATH: k=1{:}]

[MATH: z= e^{2 \cdot 1 \cdot \pi \text{i} / 12} = {\color{blue}e^{\pi \text{i} / 6}}]

We can write the given root of unity as a power of the principal root as follows:

[MATH: e^{2π\textrm{i}/3}|= e^{(2 ⋅ 2π)\textrm{i}/(2 ⋅ 3)}; = e^{4π\textrm{i}/6}; = e^{4 ⋅ π\textrm{i}/6}; = (e^{π\textrm{i}/6})^{4}]

Therefore, [MATH: p={\color{red}4}.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Product and Quotient Properties

Content:
The [MATH: n]th roots of unity have other interesting properties, which we list below, along with a proof of each result.

Content:
When proving the results, assume that [MATH: z] and [MATH: w] are [MATH: n]th roots of unity, and therefore [MATH: z^n = w^n=1.]

Content:
- A product of two [MATH: n]th roots of unity is a [MATH: n]th root of unity.

To prove this, note that
[MATH: \big(zw\big)^n= z^n\cdot w^n = 1 \cdot 1 = 1,]
which means that [MATH: zw] is also an [MATH: n]th root of unity.
- The reciprocal of an [MATH: n]th root of unity is a [MATH: n]th root of unity.

To prove this, note that
[MATH: \left(\dfrac{1}{z}\right)^n= \dfrac{1}{z^n} = \dfrac 1 1 = 1,]
which means that [MATH: \dfrac 1 z] is an [MATH: n]th root of unity too.
- The quotient of two [MATH: n]th roots of unity is a [MATH: n]th root of unity.

To prove this, note that
[MATH: \left(\dfrac{z}{w}\right)^n= \dfrac{z^n}{w^n} = \dfrac 1 1 = 1,]
which means that [MATH: \dfrac z w] is an [MATH: n]th root of unity.
- Any integer power of an [MATH: n]th root of unity is a [MATH: n]th root of unity.

To prove this, note that
[MATH: \big(z^k\big)^n= \big(z^n\big)^k = 1^k = 1,]
which means that [MATH: z^k] is an [MATH: n]th root of unity.

Item 6 — Example: Identifying True Statements Regarding Product and Quotient Properties

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: z] be a [MATH: 7]th root of unity. Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: z^7 = 1]
2. [MATH: (z+z)^7 = 1]
3. [MATH: z+z=2z] is a [MATH: 7]th root of unity

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. If [MATH: z] is a [MATH: 7]th root of unity, then (by definition), we have that
[MATH: z^7=1.]
- Statement II is false. We have
[MATH: (z + z)^{7}|= (2z)^{7}; = 2^{7} ⋅ z^{7}; = 128 ⋅ 1; = 128; ≠ 1.]
- Statement III is false. From statement II, we have that [MATH: (z+z)^7 \neq 1,] which means that [MATH: z+z=2z] is not a [MATH: 7]th root of unity.

In general, the sum of two [MATH: n]th roots of unity is not an [MATH: n]th root of unity.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Item 9 — Tutorial: Sums of Roots of Unity

Content:
The sum of all [MATH: n]th roots of unity equals zero.

Content:
To see why, recall that

Content:
- the principal [MATH: n]th root of unity is [MATH: z=e^{2\pi\text{i}/n}\neq1,] and
- any [MATH: n]th root of unity is of the form [MATH: z^k] for [MATH: k=0,1,...,n-1.]

Content:
So, the sum of all [MATH: n] roots can be calculated as the sum of the following geometric series:
[MATH: 1 + z + z^{2} + ⋯ + z^{n − 1}|= (1 − z^{n})/(1 − z); = (1 − 1)/(1 − z); = 0.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Products of Roots of Unity

Content:
The product of all [MATH: n]th roots of unity equals [MATH: 1] if [MATH: n] is odd and equals [MATH: -1] if [MATH: n] is even.

Content:
As an example, the principal fourth root of unity is

Content:
[MATH: z=e^{2\pi\text{i}/4}=e^{\pi\text{i}/2}.]

Content:
Any fourth root of unity is of the form [MATH: z^k] for [MATH: k=0,1,2,3.] Also, we have [MATH: z^4=1.]

Content:
Therefore, the product of all four roots of unity is

Content:
[MATH: z^{0} ⋅ z^{1} ⋅ z^{2} ⋅ z^{3}|= z^{0 + 1 + 2 + 3}; = z^{6}; = z^{4} ⋅ z^{2}; = 1 ⋅ (e^{π\textrm{i}/2})^{2}; = e^{π\textrm{i}}; = − 1.]

Content:

Item 11 — Example: Identifying True Statements Regarding Sums and Products

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the principal cube root of unity is

[MATH: z=e^{2\pi\text{i}/3},]

and that any cube root of unity is of the form [MATH: z^k] for [MATH: k=0,1,2.] Also, we have [MATH: z^3=1.]

Therefore, the product of all three roots is

[MATH: z^{0} ⋅ z^{1} ⋅ z^{2}|= z^{0 + 1 + 2}; = z^{3}; = 1.]
